This triad—psychosis, cognitive decline, and movement disorder—strongly suggests a neurodegenerative or metabolic basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuitopathy. Huntington disease is top-ranked due to its classic presentation of chorea, psychiatric symptoms (irritability, psychosis), dysarthria, dysphagia, and progressive dementia; age of onset often 30–50 years, and duration aligns. Wilson disease is highly plausible given its neuropsychiatric onset (often before liver signs), dysarthria, dystonia/chorea, dysphagia, and cognitive decline—especially if undiagnosed in young adulthood; serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hr urinary copper are critical tests. Neuroacanthocytosis (e.g., chorea-acanthocytosis) fits well: adult-onset orofacial/buccolingual dyskinesias (causing dysphagia and dysarthria), self-mutilation (not reported but common), psychosis, and cognitive decline; acanthocytes on peripheral smear and CK elevation support it. FTD-MND variant is less common but possible—particularly behavioral variant FTD with motor neuron involvement causing bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria) and parkinsonism, though prominent auditory hallucinations are atypical. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is lower-confidence: while it causes psychosis, movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias), dysphagia, and speech changes, its typical course is subacute (weeks-months), not chronic over a year, and usually includes seizures, autonomic instability, or catatonia—none mentioned; however, atypical, protracted cases exist, warranting CSF NMDAR antibody testing."}

Wilson disease is top-ranked due to its classic triad: neuropsychiatric manifestations (often preceding hepatic signs), movement disorders (e.g., dystonia, tremor), and bulbar involvement (dysphagia, dysarthria); the unasked but highly relevant Kayser–Fleischer ring (golden-brown corneal ring) would be confirmatory—its absence was not documented, leaving high suspicion intact. Huntington disease fits well with chorea, dysarthria, dysphagia, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms, though auditory hallucinations are less typical and onset is usually earlier; still highly plausible. NPSLE is included given its multisystem nature, potential for psychosis, movement disorders (chorea), dysphagia (brainstem/cranial nerve involvement), and cognitive dysfunction—especially in young-to-middle-aged adults—but typically has systemic inflammatory markers and fluctuating course. Early-onset Alzheimer disease is less likely given prominent motor and bulbar features early on, though atypical variants (e.g., corticobasal syndrome or frontotemporal dementia mimics) can present with mixed neuropsychiatric and motor signs; confidence is reduced by relative rarity of hallucinations and dysphagia in pure AD. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is considered due to psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias), speech disturbance, and autonomic/brainstem involvement—but its typical presentation is subacute (weeks), not chronic (1 year), and often includes seizures, catatonia, or autonomic instability; low confidence reflects temporal mismatch and lack of reported prodrome or tumor association."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Wilson disease", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Huntington disease", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Neurosyphilis (tertiary or general paresis)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis)", "confidence": 0.62}, {"diagnosis": "Fahr disease (primary familial brain calcification)", "confidence": 0.54}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.582, "reasoning": "The constellation of neuropsychiatric symptoms (irritability, auditory hallucinations, memory decline), dysphagia, dysarthria, and involuntary movements over a subacute-to-chronic course strongly suggests a progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder with basal ganglia and cortical involvement. Wilson disease is top-ranked due to its classic triad: psychiatric manifestations (often early), movement disorders (dystonia, tremor, dysarthria, dysphagia), and cognitive decline—plus the high pretest probability given age of onset (~teens–30s) and the unasked but highly relevant Kayser-Fleischer ring and hepatic abnormalities (which were not confirmed but remain critical to rule out). Huntington disease fits well with chorea, dysarthria, dysphagia, psychiatric symptoms, and dementia—but typically lacks prominent auditory hallucinations and has stronger family history; age of onset is often later (30–50), though juvenile forms exist. Neurosyphilis remains plausible given its 'great imitator' status, with tabes dorsalis or general paresis causing psychosis, movement disorder, and bulbar signs—though rapid progression over 1 year is atypical, and serologic testing would be definitive. Autoimmune encephalitis (especially anti-NMDAR) can present with psychosis, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias, catatonia), dysphagia, and autonomic instability—though dysphagia is less common early, and the 1-year chronicity is longer than typical untreated cases. Fahr disease presents with basal ganglia calcifications leading to parkinsonism, dystonia, psychosis, and cognitive decline, but dysphagia and prominent auditory hallucinations are less characteristic, and calcifications are usually incidental or slowly progressive—making it lower confidence. Other considerations (e.g., mitochondrial disorders, prion disease, late-onset lysosomal storage diseases) were excluded due to lack of supporting features (e.g., myoclonus, rapid decline, systemic stigmata)."}
